title: Series and Parallel L-C-R Circuits in Alternating Current
short_intro: An L-C-R circuit consists of a resistor, an inductor, and a capacitor connected in series or parallel across an alternating voltage source. It exhibits resonance phenomena governed by the interplay of resistance, inductive reactance, and capacitive reactance.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Series LCR circuit impedance, resonance frequency, phase angle, and basic power factor concepts.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Parallel LCR resonance, quality factor (Q-factor), sharpness of resonance, bandwidth, and vector/phasor analysis of complex AC networks.

prerequisites: Alternating current fundamentals and phasor representation
Reactance of pure resistors, inductors, and capacitors
Complex numbers and vector addition for harmonic oscillations

concept_notes.heading: Impedance and Phasor Diagram of Series L-C-R Circuit
bullets: The total opposition to AC flow in a series L-C-R circuit is called impedance (Z), combining resistance R and net reactance X = X<sub>L</sub> - X<sub>C</sub>.
Voltage leads current by a phase angle φ when X<sub>L</sub> > X<sub>C</sub> (inductive circuit) and lags when X<sub>L</sub> < X<sub>C</sub> (capacitive circuit).
The impedance is expressed vectorially as Z = R + j(X<sub>L</sub> - X<sub>C</sub>) with magnitude Z = sqrt{R<sup>2</sup> + (X<sub>L</sub> - X<sub>C</sub>)<sup>2</sup>}.

concept_notes.heading: Series Resonance and Resonance Frequency
bullets: Resonance occurs in a series L-C-R circuit when the inductive reactance equals the capacitive reactance (X<sub>L</sub> = X<sub>C</sub>).
At resonance, the net reactance is zero, impedance is minimum (Z = R), and current is maximum for a given voltage source.
The angular resonance frequency is given by omega_0 = 1/sqrt{LC}, making the current strictly in phase with the applied voltage (φ = 0).

concept_notes.heading: Quality Factor (Q-factor) and Selectivity
bullets: The Q-factor of a series resonant circuit measures the sharpness of resonance and voltage magnification across L or C relative to R.
It is defined as the ratio of resonant inductive reactance (or capacitive reactance) to the circuit resistance: Q = omega_0 L / R = 1 / (omega_0 C R).
A high Q-factor signifies a narrow bandwidth and high selectivity, crucial in radio tuning circuits.

concept_notes.heading: Parallel L-C-R (Rejector) Circuit
bullets: In a parallel L-C-R circuit, an inductor (with resistance r) and a capacitor are connected in parallel across an AC source.
At parallel resonance, the circuit offers maximum impedance to the source and draws minimum (or nearly zero) current.
The parallel resonant frequency is slightly different from the series case, given by omega_0 = sqrt{ rac{1}{LC} -  rac{r^2}{L^2}}.

derivations.title: Impedance and Phase Angle of Series L-C-R Circuit
derivations.conditions: AC voltage V = V_0 sin(omega t) applied across series combination of R, L, and C
steps: Write the potential drops across R, L, and C as V_R = I R (in phase with I), V_L = I X_L (leading I by 90°), and V_C = I X_C (lagging I by 90°).
Apply Kirchhoff's voltage law using phasor addition: V_0^2 = V_{R0}^2 + (V_{L0} - V_{C0})^2.
Substitute V_0 = I_0 Z, V_{R0} = I_0 R, V_{L0} = I_0 X_L, and V_{C0} = I_0 X_C into the equation and divide by I_0^2.
Obtain the impedance magnitude and phase angle using 	an(phi) =  rac{X_L - X_C}{R}.
derivations.result: Z = sqrt{R^2 + (omega L -  rac{1}{omega C})^2} 	ext{ and } phi = 	an^{-1}left( rac{omega L -  rac{1}{omega C}}{R}ight)

derivations.title: Bandwidth and Quality Factor of Series L-C-R Circuit
derivations.conditions: Series resonant circuit driven by a constant voltage source of variable frequency
steps: Define bandwidth (Delta omega) as the frequency interval between the two half-power points where current drops to 1/sqrt{2} of its maximum value.
Set the total impedance at half-power frequencies to Z = sqrt{2} R, meaning |omega L -  rac{1}{omega C}| = R.
Solve the resulting quadratic equations for the lower (omega_1) and upper (omega_2) cutoff frequencies: omega_2 - omega_1 =  rac{R}{L}.
Express the quality factor as Q =  rac{omega_0}{Delta omega} =  rac{omega_0 L}{R}.
derivations.result: Q =  rac{omega_0 L}{R} =  rac{1}{omega_0 C R} 	ext{ and } Delta omega =  rac{R}{L}

formula_sheet.name: Inductive Reactance
formula_sheet.equation_html: X_L = omega L = 2 pi f L

formula_sheet.name: Capacitive Reactance
formula_sheet.equation_html: X_C =  rac{1}{omega C} =  rac{1}{2 pi f C}

formula_sheet.name: Series Impedance
formula_sheet.variables: R = resistance, X_L = inductive reactance, X_C = capacitive reactance

formula_sheet.name: Quality Factor
formula_sheet.equation_html: Q =  rac{omega_0 L}{R} =  rac{1}{omega_0 C R}
formula_sheet.variables: omega_0 = resonant angular frequency, L = inductance, C = capacitance, R = resistance

formula_sheet.name: Average Power Dissipation
formula_sheet.variables: V_{rms} = root mean square voltage, I_{rms} = root mean square current, cos(phi) = power factor

formula_sheet.name: Parallel Resonance Frequency
formula_sheet.variables: r = internal resistance of inductor, L = inductance, C = capacitance
formula_sheet.conditions: Parallel L-C-R circuit with lossy inductor

graphs_and_experiments.title: Current vs Frequency Resonance Curve
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A bell-shaped curve plotting root-mean-square current (I_{rms}) on the y-axis against AC frequency (f) on the x-axis for different values of resistance R.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Shows a sharp peak at f = f_0. Lower resistance curves yield narrower, taller peaks (high Q-factor), while higher resistance curves flatten out.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Frequently used in conceptual MCQs asking how resistance affects sharpness of resonance and peak current.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Phasor Diagram of Series L-C-R Circuit
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A vector diagram showing current phasor along the reference axis, V_R in phase, V_L pointing 90° ahead, V_C pointing 90° behind, and resultant voltage V vectorially.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Visualizes Kirchhoff's voltage law in alternating current and clearly defines the phase angle φ between voltage and current.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Tested in numericals determining phase lag/lead and instantaneous voltage equations.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Impedance vs Frequency Curve
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A hyperbolic-looking V-shaped curve plotting impedance Z on the y-axis versus frequency f on the x-axis, achieving a minimum value equal to R at f_0.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Demonstrates that total impedance drops to its lowest value at resonance because reactive components cancel out completely.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Tested in questions concerning minimum impedance and maximum current conditions in radio receivers.

solved_numericals.question: A series L-C-R circuit contains a resistance of 10 Omega, an inductance of 0.2 H, and a capacitance of 50 muF connected to a 200 V, 50 Hz AC supply. Calculate the impedance of the circuit.
solution_steps: Calculate inductive reactance: X_L = 2 pi f L = 2 	imes pi 	imes 50 	imes 0.2 = 62.8 Omega.
Calculate capacitive reactance: X_C =  rac{1}{2 pi f C} =  rac{1}{2 	imes pi 	imes 50 	imes 50 	imes 10^{-6}} = 63.66 Omega.
Compute net reactance: X = X_L - X_C = 62.8 - 63.66 = -0.86 Omega.
Calculate total impedance: Z = sqrt{R^2 + X^2} = sqrt{10^2 + (-0.86)^2} approx sqrt{100 + 0.74} = 10.04 Omega.

solved_numericals.question: A series L-C-R circuit with L = 2 H, C = 32 muF, and R = 10 Omega is driven by a variable frequency source of peak voltage 100 V. Find the resonant frequency, the maximum current at resonance, and the quality factor of the circuit.
solution_steps: Calculate resonant angular frequency: omega_0 =  rac{1}{sqrt{LC}} =  rac{1}{sqrt{2 	imes 32 	imes 10^{-6}}} =  rac{1}{sqrt{64 	imes 10^{-6}}} =  rac{1}{8 	imes 10^{-3}} = 125 	ext{ rad/s}.
Convert to linear frequency: f_0 =  rac{omega_0}{2 pi} =  rac{125}{2 pi} approx 19.89 	ext{ Hz}.
Calculate maximum current at resonance: I_{0,max} =  rac{V_0}{R} =  rac{100}{10} = 10 	ext{ A}.
Calculate Q-factor: Q =  rac{omega_0 L}{R} =  rac{125 	imes 2}{10} = 25.

solved_numericals.question: In a parallel L-C-R circuit, L = 5 H, C = 2 muF, and the internal resistance of the inductor is r = 20 Omega. Determine the parallel resonance frequency and the dynamic impedance of the circuit at resonance.
solution_steps: Calculate parallel resonance angular frequency: omega_0 = sqrt{ rac{1}{LC} -  rac{r^2}{L^2}} = sqrt{ rac{1}{5 	imes 2 	imes 10^{-6}} -  rac{20^2}{5^2}}.
Evaluate terms under root:  rac{1}{10^{-5}} = 10^5 = 100,000 	ext{ and }  rac{400}{25} = 16.
Find omega_0 = sqrt{100,000 - 16} approx sqrt{100,000} approx 316.22 	ext{ rad/s}.
Calculate dynamic impedance at resonance: Z_d =  rac{L}{C r} =  rac{5}{(2 	imes 10^{-6}) 	imes 20} =  rac{5}{4 	imes 10^{-5}} = 125,000 Omega = 125 	ext{ k}Omega.

assumptions_and_limitations: Components are assumed to be ideal (pure R, pure L, pure C) except where internal resistance of inductors is explicitly factored into PGT derivations.
The source voltage is assumed to be perfectly sinusoidal with single fixed frequency or smoothly variable frequency.
Stray capacitances and mutual inductances connecting circuit wiring are neglected in standard theoretical analysis.

common_misconceptions.wrong: At series resonance, the voltage across the inductor and capacitor individually is zero.
common_misconceptions.correct: Individual voltages V_L and V_C are non-zero and can be very large, but they are equal in magnitude and 180° out of phase, thus canceling each other out in the total circuit sum.
common_misconceptions.why: Cancellation happens across the reactive pair (V_L - V_C = 0), but each component still sustains a large potential drop equal to Q times the supply voltage.

common_misconceptions.wrong: The impedance of a series L-C-R circuit is simply the arithmetic sum of R, X_L, and X_C.
common_misconceptions.correct: Impedance is the vector (phasor) sum Z = sqrt{R^2 + (X_L - X_C)^2}, because reactive voltages maintain a 90° phase difference relative to resistive voltage.
common_misconceptions.why: Algebraic addition ignores the phase quadrature between resistive and reactive voltage drops.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Parallel resonance occurs at exactly the same frequency as series resonance (omega_0 = 1/sqrt{LC}).
common_misconceptions.correct: Parallel resonance frequency is affected by the ohmic resistance of the inductor, shifting the resonance condition slightly.
common_misconceptions.why: The exact parallel resonance formula includes a damping term dependent on the inductor's internal resistance r.

quick_revision: Series resonance condition: X_L = X_C, yielding minimum impedance Z = R and maximum current.
Resonant frequency formula: f_0 =  rac{1}{2 pi sqrt{LC}}.
Power factor equals cos(phi) = R/Z, becoming unity at resonance.
Q-factor represents voltage magnification and selectivity, given by Q =  rac{omega_0 L}{R}.
Parallel LCR circuit acts as a rejector circuit offering maximum impedance at resonance.
